question: The team notices that the pipeline takes 25 minutes. All jobs are chained sequentially through stages. What is the first optimization step?

options.text: Reduce expire_in for artifacts
options.explanation: Artifact retention time does not affect pipeline execution speed.

options.text: Move all jobs into a single stage
options.explanation: This would make all jobs parallel without considering dependencies. Tests would run before the build, causing errors.

options.text: Add more Runners
options.explanation: More Runners won't help if jobs run sequentially — they'll just wait in the queue.

options.text: Use needs to create a DAG — jobs will start immediately after their dependencies, not wait for the entire stage
options.explanation: needs breaks the rigid tie to stages. A job starts as soon as its direct dependencies are ready, not when the entire stage finishes. This is the main lever for speedup.

question: What is GIT_DEPTH: '1' in the context of CI/CD and why use it?

options.text: Limit the number of parallel jobs in the pipeline
options.explanation: GIT_DEPTH controls git clone depth, not the number of jobs.

options.text: Set the pipeline priority — 1 means the highest priority
options.explanation: GIT_DEPTH is not related to priority. It controls git clone depth.

options.text: Allow only one nesting level in .gitlab-ci.yml
options.explanation: This is not an existing GitLab CI configuration parameter.

options.text: Download only the last commit without history — speeds up clone in projects with long history
options.explanation: A shallow clone with depth=1 downloads only the current code state. For most CI jobs, full history is not needed, and its absence saves minutes on clone.

question: In a monorepo there are frontend and backend. When only README.md changes, all tests run — frontend, backend, e2e. How to fix this?

options.text: Use rules:changes with paths to the corresponding directories — the job runs only when files in those paths change
options.explanation: rules:changes allows running a job only when files at specified paths change. test:frontend — when src/frontend/** changes, test:backend — when src/backend/** changes.

options.text: Use only: changes instead of rules:changes
options.explanation: only/except is deprecated syntax. GitLab recommends using rules, which is more flexible.

options.text: Create separate repositories for each component
options.explanation: Splitting into repositories would solve the symptom but create new coordination problems. GitLab CI has tools for monorepos.

options.text: Add when: manual for all tests
options.explanation: Manual triggering is not automation. Developers will forget to run tests.

question: How does extends differ from YAML anchors (&/*) when organizing .gitlab-ci.yml?

options.text: extends supports includes from other files, works with multiple parents, and is more readable; YAML anchors don't work with includes
options.explanation: The key difference: YAML anchors are processed by the YAML parser before GitLab, so they don't work with include. extends is a GitLab CI feature processed after all includes are assembled.

options.text: extends works slower — GitLab must process inheritance before running
options.explanation: Config processing speed is negligible and not a valid argument for choosing an approach.

options.text: extends only works with jobs in the same file, anchors work across all includes
options.explanation: The opposite is true. extends works with jobs from any files connected via include. Anchors are limited to a single file.

options.text: YAML anchors support conditional inheritance through rules, extends does not
options.explanation: Both approaches work equally with rules. That is not the difference.

question: A team wants to switch to trunk-based development. What does this mean for the development process?

options.text: Every commit is automatically deployed to production
options.explanation: Not necessarily. Trunk-based development is about code integration, not auto-deploy to prod. Feature flags allow deploying without enabling functionality.

options.text: Incomplete code is hidden behind feature flags rather than waiting in a separate branch
options.explanation: Feature flags are a key tool of trunk-based development. Code is deployed but functionality is enabled separately.

options.text: Feature branches live no more than 1-2 days
options.explanation: Short-lived branches reduce the risk of conflicts and allow faster feedback from CI.

options.text: All developers commit to main at least once a day
options.explanation: Trunk-based development assumes frequent small integrations into the main branch instead of long-lived feature branches.

question: What is DORA Lead Time for Changes and why is this metric important?

options.text: Time to restore service after an incident
options.explanation: This is the Time to Restore Service (MTTR) metric, not Lead Time for Changes.

options.text: Execution time of the longest job in the pipeline
options.explanation: This is the time of a specific job, not the end-to-end delivery metric.

options.text: Time for Merge Request code review — how long an MR waits for approval
options.explanation: Review time is part of Lead Time, but the metric is broader — from commit to production.

options.text: Time from commit in main to deployment in production — shows the speed of value delivery
options.explanation: Lead Time measures the entire journey: code written -> running in production. Elite teams achieve < 1 hour. This directly impacts product competitiveness.

question: You have a pipeline with 8 jobs. After optimization via needs it's faster, but the 'build:docker' job still takes 12 minutes. Which approaches would help speed it up specifically?

options.text: This requires a special license
options.explanation: The listed technologies have open-source versions.

options.text: Use BuildKit with Docker image layer caching between runs
options.explanation: Docker layer cache is the main tool for speeding up image builds. BuildKit can cache layers in a registry or locally on the Runner.

options.text: Reduce GIT_DEPTH to 1 specifically for this job
options.explanation: If build:docker doesn't need git history (only files), a shallow clone saves time on git operations.

options.text: Add parallel: 4 to the build:docker job
options.explanation: parallel runs N copies of the same job with different $CI_NODE_INDEX values. For building a single Docker image this won't help — you can't build one image in parallel.

options.text: Optimize the Dockerfile: combine RUN commands, properly order layers (frequently changing ones at the end)
options.explanation: Layer order in the Dockerfile is critical for caching. COPY package.json and npm install should come before COPY src/ — otherwise cache is invalidated on every code change.

question: How to properly structure .gitlab-ci.yml for a large project with build, test, security scan, and deploy?

options.text: One .gitlab-ci.yml file with comment separators
options.explanation: Comments help readability but don't solve the scaling problem. 1000 lines with comments are still hard to maintain.

options.text: Use only YAML anchors for DRY — this is the most compact approach
options.explanation: YAML anchors don't work across include files. When splitting into files, you'll have to use extends.

options.text: Split logic into .gitlab/ci/*.yml files and connect via include; the main file contains only stages and global variables
options.explanation: Separation by responsibility through include makes each file understandable, reduces conflicts during parallel team work, and simplifies navigation.

options.text: Create a separate repository for CI/CD configs
options.explanation: A separate repository creates a version synchronization problem between code and CI config. Config should live alongside code.

question: What is GitOps and how does it differ from classical CI/CD deployment?

options.text: GitOps is storing .gitlab-ci.yml in a separate repository
options.explanation: This is not GitOps. Storing CI config separately is more of an anti-pattern.

options.text: In GitOps the pipeline updates git manifests, and the cluster itself (via ArgoCD/Flux) applies changes; in the classical approach the pipeline deploys directly
options.explanation: GitOps inverts the direction: instead of CI pushing to the cluster, the cluster pulls from git. Git becomes the single source of truth for the desired state.

options.text: GitOps requires using only git tags for deployment, no branches
options.explanation: GitOps does not restrict the source of changes. Typically the image tag in Helm values.yaml is changed — this can happen from any branch.

options.text: GitOps is a marketing term for deployment via git push
options.explanation: GitOps is an architectural pattern with concrete principles: declarativeness, versioning, automatic synchronization, a control loop closure system.

question: You write a .deploy-template with variables $APP_NAME and $K8S_NAMESPACE. The deploy:staging and deploy:production jobs inherit it, but with different variables. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Create a separate .yml file for each environment — staging.yml, production.yml
options.explanation: This reduces readability and creates duplication. One template with parameters is better than several similar files.

options.text: Duplicate the entire script in each job, changing only the variables
options.explanation: This violates DRY. Changing deploy logic requires updating all places — high risk of errors.

options.text: Pass variables via trigger: — this mechanism is designed for passing parameters
options.explanation: trigger launches a child pipeline. For parameterizing jobs within the same pipeline, use extends with variables.

options.text: Use extends: .deploy-template and override variables through variables in each job
options.explanation: The correct pattern. The script is in one template, environment variables are in child jobs. Change deploy logic in one place — it changes everywhere.

question: The DORA Change Failure Rate metric for the team is 30%. What does this mean and what should be done?

options.text: Reduce deployment frequency — deploy less often, fewer problems
options.explanation: This is counterintuitive but wrong. Deploy less often -> larger batches of changes -> harder to roll back -> higher risk. Better to deploy more often, but in smaller increments.

options.text: 30% of deployments lead to incidents or require a hotfix — this is 'medium' level by DORA
options.explanation: Change Failure Rate of 30% means: every third deployment causes problems. By DORA benchmark: elite < 5%, high < 10%, medium 15-45%.

options.text: Implement canary deployments or blue-green deployment to reduce risk
options.explanation: Gradual rollout catches the problem at a small traffic percentage and rolls back before the incident affects all users.

options.text: Strengthen automated testing before deployment, especially integration tests
options.explanation: High CFR often means insufficient test coverage. Tests should catch problems before prod, not after.

question: What does the 'Fail Fast' principle mean in the context of a pipeline and how to implement it correctly?

options.text: The pipeline should fail as often as possible to detect more errors
options.explanation: The goal is not the number of failures but the speed of problem detection. The pipeline should be reliable, not unstable.

options.text: Use allow_failure: true for all jobs — the pipeline never blocks work
options.explanation: allow_failure: true for all jobs means checks verify nothing. This is the complete opposite of Fail Fast.

options.text: The fastest and cheapest checks (linter, static analysis) should come first — if they fail, expensive tests won't run
options.explanation: A 30-second linter should come before 15-minute e2e tests. If the code doesn't compile, there's no point running tests. The developer gets feedback faster.

options.text: Run all jobs in parallel without dependencies — this way the first error will be found faster
options.explanation: Running tests in parallel with the build will cause a 'no artifacts' error. Dependencies are needed, they just need to be optimized.

question: A team has set up feature flags for new functionality. Code is deployed to prod, flag is off. What advantages does this approach have over a feature branch?

options.text: No need to write tests — the flag can just be turned off if there are problems
options.explanation: Feature flags don't replace tests. Code with a flag must still be covered by tests — otherwise unexpected bugs will appear when the flag is enabled.

options.text: You can test on real traffic with gradual enablement (1% -> 10% -> 100%)
options.explanation: Canary release via feature flags is a powerful technique. You can enable a feature for 1% of users, look at metrics, and only then expand.

options.text: Code in main goes through real CI/CD and integrates with the rest of the code continuously
options.explanation: A feature branch accumulates divergence from main. Flagged code is always in main — no merge conflicts.

options.text: Instant rollback: turn off the flag — rolled back, without a new deployment
options.explanation: This is one of the main advantages. Time to Restore for a flag problem is seconds, not minutes for a new deployment.

question: You are setting up pipeline monitoring. You need to receive Slack notifications only when the pipeline fails on the main branch. Which configuration is correct?

options.text: when: on_failure without rules — notification on any failure in any branch
options.explanation: Notifications about every feature branch failure create noise. It's critical to monitor main specifically.

options.text: only: [master] — old syntax, but works for branch restriction
options.explanation: only/except are deprecated. Additionally, you still need to specify when: on_failure — only doesn't control success/failure conditions.

options.text: stage: .post without additional conditions — the .post stage always runs on errors
options.explanation: .post runs after other stages, but not automatically on errors. Without when: on_failure the job only runs when the pipeline succeeds.

options.text: rules: [{if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH', when: on_failure}] — notification only on main branch failure
options.explanation: The combination of if (branch condition) and when: on_failure precisely configures the trigger. Noise from feature branches doesn't interfere.

question: The project is growing: 15 developers, 3 teams, monorepo. The pipeline takes 45 minutes. Which changes will have the biggest effect?

options.text: rules:changes — run tests only for changed components
options.explanation: With 3 teams, developers often change only their own component. rules:changes will let the backend team avoid waiting for frontend tests.

options.text: GIT_DEPTH: '1' globally — speed up clone on all jobs
options.explanation: In a large project, git history can take significant time. Shallow clone speeds up every job.

options.text: Split the monorepo into separate repositories — this is the only scalable solution
options.explanation: Splitting solves the pipeline problem but creates coordination problems between teams. Optimizing the monorepo via rules:changes is more effective.

options.text: Distributed cache (S3/GCS) for sharing cache between Runners
options.explanation: 15 developers = many parallel pipelines = many Runners. Without distributed cache, each Runner installs dependencies from scratch.
